title: Logging, alerting and exceptional conditions
summary: A09 and A10: log the security events that matter without logging secrets, turn them into alerts a person will see, and keep error paths failing closed. Write the brute-force and credential-stuffing detector a SOC would run.

steps.title: The attack nobody saw
body: Most breaches are found by someone else (a customer, a researcher, a journalist) weeks after they started. **A09:2025 Security Logging and Alerting Failures** is about closing that gap:

- **Log** security-relevant events, with who, what, from where and the result: sign-ins and failures, MFA changes, password resets, permission changes, access denied (403/404 on other users' objects), input validation failures, 429s, admin actions, exports.
- **Do not log secrets**: passwords (even wrong ones: they are often the right password for another site), tokens, session ids, full card numbers, API keys. Log a user id and a request id instead.
- **Encode** what you log (the STRIDE lesson's forged line), use structured logging, and send it somewhere an attacker on the box cannot edit.
- **Alert**: a log nobody reads is not monitoring. A few precise alerts that a person acts on beat a thousand dashboards.

A10 (exceptional conditions) is the code side of the same coin: when the rate limiter's store is down, when the token can't be parsed, when the permissions service times out, the code must fail **closed** and **log** that it did.

steps.prompt: Log it, or keep it out of the log?
items: Failed sign-in: username, source address, time
The rate limiter rejecting a client with 429
The password from a failed sign-in
A full card number from the checkout form

steps.title: From events to alerts
body: Two classic detection rules over sign-in events:
brute force:   one username,  >= 5 failures within 60 seconds        -> "brute-force carol"
stuffing:      one address,   failures for >= 4 different usernames within 60 seconds -> "stuffing 203.0.113.9"

In production these run in a SIEM (Microsoft Sentinel's KQL, Splunk's SPL, Elastic rules), with thresholds tuned on real traffic so they fire on attacks and not on Monday mornings. A **sliding window** (any 60 seconds, not each calendar minute) matters: an attack spread across 10:00:50 to 10:01:20 must not escape by straddling a minute boundary.
| summarize Failures = count(), Users = dcount(UserPrincipalName) by IPAddress, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)

steps.prompt: A failed-login alert fires 300 times a day, mostly on users who mistype their password once or twice. The team mutes it. What is the better fix?
options: Tune the rule (more failures, a sliding window, per-address and per-account variants) so it fires on attack patterns, and route it to someone who must act
Keep it muted and review the dashboard weekly
Alert on every single failed login
Stop logging failed logins to save money
steps.explain: A muted alert is the same as no alert. Precision is what keeps people reading them.

steps.title: Detect brute force and credential stuffing
prompt: Write `List<string> Alerts(List<LoginEvent> events)`. `record LoginEvent(DateTime At, string Ip, string Username, bool Success)` is given. Events may arrive in any order. Only failures (`Success == false`) count.
- `"brute-force <username>"` when one username has **5 or more** failures within **any 60-second window** (the last minus the first at most 60 seconds);
- `"stuffing <ip>"` when one address has failures for **4 or more different usernames** within any 60-second window;
- each alert at most once; the list sorted with ordinal string order.
solution: var users = list.Skip(i).TakeWhile(e => e.At - list[i].At <= TimeSpan.FromSeconds(60)).Select(e => e.Username).Distinct().Count();
hints: Keep only failures and sort them by time. Then group: by `Username` for brute force, by `Ip` for stuffing.
Brute force: in a time-sorted group, 5 failures within 60 s exist when some `list[i + 4].At - list[i].At <= 60 s`.
Stuffing: from each event, take the following events while they are within 60 s and count the distinct usernames.
template: LoginEvent F(int s, string ip, string user) => new(t0.AddSeconds(s), ip, user, false);
Dojo.Eq("5 failures for carol in 28 s, across a minute boundary", new List<string> { "brute-force carol" }, Alerts(brute));
Dojo.Eq("5 failures spread over 80 s do not alert", new List<string>(), Alerts(slow));
var mixed = new List<LoginEvent>(brute) { new(t0.AddSeconds(3), "198.51.100.4", "carol", true) };
Dojo.Eq("order does not matter, successes do not count", new List<string> { "brute-force carol" }, Alerts(mixed));
Dojo.Eq("4 usernames from one address in 30 s", new List<string> { "stuffing 203.0.113.9" }, Alerts(stuffing));
Dojo.Eq("4 usernames over 95 s do not alert", new List<string>(), Alerts(spread));
Dojo.Eq("both alerts, sorted", new List<string> { "brute-force carol", "stuffing 203.0.113.9" }, Alerts(both));
var typos = new List<LoginEvent> { F(0, "192.0.2.1", "ada"), F(5, "192.0.2.1", "ada"), new(t0.AddSeconds(9), "192.0.2.1", "ada", true) };
Dojo.Eq("two typos then a success: nothing", new List<string>(), Alerts(typos));
record LoginEvent(DateTime At, string Ip, string Username, bool Success);
